Made for curious humans. Bad summaries welcome.Social Graphs · Week 7 ↗
The science under the squeeze

One passage.
Three cuts.

You squeeze a real Wikipedia passage into 30 words, then 10, then 3. After every keystroke, two search systems rank all 303 articles, and you watch where the source article lands. At the end your round is drawn over the same squeeze run automatically on every article.

Keyword search · TF-IDF
Compares shared words, giving more weight to terms that are rare in this 303-article corpus. While you type, each word shows its share of the source article’s score; stop words and words the corpus never uses are ignored.
Semantic search · MiniLM
Encodes your words as a normalized 384-dimensional vector and ranks articles by cosine similarity to their best matching passage (60 words by default) or to whole-page averages.
Taboo mode
Bans the passage’s five highest-weight TF-IDF words: the rarest words keyword search would lean on. You have to say it differently, which is the vocabulary mismatch dense retrieval is meant to solve.
The corpus-wide evidence
For every article, a fixed sentence (18–45 words, title replaced by “someone”) is squeezed automatically to 30, 20, 10, 5, 3, 2 and 1 words by three rules: keep the first N words, keep the rarest N, or ban the rarest five and keep the rarest N of the rest. The chart shows the median rank and the middle half. The robot only deletes words; it never paraphrases.
What the score means
A cosine score compares vectors within one method. It is not confidence, a probability, or a percentage of meaning retained. A high score can still retrieve the wrong article.
What one round can show
One round is a case study, not a benchmark. Use the same text and switch retrieval units, or switch between your 30, 10 and 3 words, for controlled comparisons.

Source: 303 Wikipedia articles from the course’s frozen August 26, 2026 snapshot. Prompts are exact excerpts with selected names replaced by “someone”; originals and attribution appear at the reveal. Wikipedia text is available under CC BY-SA 4.0.

Text model: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (Apache 2.0). Article vectors were prepared with Sentence Transformers; live text queries use the quantized ONNX version of the same encoder in your browser. Stored MiniLM vectors use signed-byte quantization and are renormalized for scoring, so rankings are approximate. TF-IDF uses English stop words, sublinear term frequency, unigrams, and L2 normalization. All models and data are served with this page. Your words stay in this tab; there is no upload or online room.
